subject: English
passage: Helsinki has strikingly high per-capita library visits, but simply replicating a feature of Helsinki associated with this usage—e.g., its extensive free equipment lending—may be insufficient to increase library visits in other cities. As information scholar Amara Kamau argues, our understanding of individuals' decision-making about whether to visit a library is insufficiently robust: some studies emphasize the role of perceived welcome, others the role of convenient hours, and so on. But decisions about library use are made in complex contexts in which multiple conditions and needs inform individuals' choices.
prompt: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To describe the effect of free equipment lending on any given city's library usage
choices.B: To present a claim about how individuals' decision-making about visiting libraries can be improved
choices.C: To discuss the difficulty of identifying a reliable way to increase library visits in any given city
choices.D: To explain why it is challenging to compare the amount of library usage in different cities

explanation:
Choice C is the best answer because it most accurately describes the main purpose of the text, which is to discuss the difficulty of identifying a reliable way to increase library visits in any given city. The text begins by noting that Helsinki has strikingly high per-capita library visits but cautions that simply replicating one of Helsinki's features associated with this usage, such as its extensive free equipment lending, may not be sufficient to increase library visits in other cities. The text then presents Amara Kamau's argument that our understanding of what drives individuals' decisions about whether to visit a library is insufficiently robust, with some studies emphasizing perceived welcome, others emphasizing convenient hours, and so on. The text concludes by noting that decisions about library use are made in complex contexts in which multiple conditions and needs inform individuals' choices. Taken together, these points convey the difficulty of identifying a reliable method to increase library visits: simply copying a feature from a heavily used library system may not work because visit decisions are influenced by multiple, complex factors that researchers don't yet fully understand.

Why D is incorrect:

Choice D is incorrect because the text doesn't discuss comparing the amount of library usage in different cities. While the text does mention that Helsinki has high per-capita library visits, it uses this fact as a starting point for discussing the difficulty of increasing library visits in other cities by replicating Helsinki's features, not as part of an explanation about why it's challenging to compare usage amounts across cities.
